utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll now be proceeding with our hearings, and I would like to greet the accused, the Defence, the Prosecution, and everyone else assisting us. First of all, I have a brief oral decision that I would like to read out. It is a request for clarification that concerns the Stojic Defence's request to have the English translation of document P 05955 corrected. On the 18th of July, 2008, the Stojic Defence filed a request to have the English translation of document P 05955 corrected. This document was admitted into evidence on the 11th of December, 2007, pursuant to a decision on the request for admission into evidence of documents presented by the Prosecution. To requests relating to the HVO Herceg-Bosna concerned. The Stojic Defence seems to be requesting that a new translation of the entire document, P 05955, be made given that there is allegedly an error that -- in the date that the document bears at least in the English translation of the document. The Chamber would like the Stojic Defence to specify whether it is requesting a new translation of the entire document or whether it is simply requesting that CLSS verify the date of the document. So what is Ms. Nozica's position?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. To be quite specific, the Stojic Defence only wanted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Speak a little more loudly because the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that warning. Good day once again, Your Honours. Good day to everyone in the courtroom. The Stojic Defence requested that the date alone be translated. I can't remember the problem. I think it was the month, that's obvious in the translation and in the original document, but I think it would be good to have an accurate translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Thank you. We'll check the date in that case. As far as the witness who is to appear is concerned, Mr. Martin Raguz, I believe that the Prlic Defence needs four hours, the other members of the Defence will have two hours, and the Prosecution will have four hours. Is that correct, Mr. Karnavas, and let me greet you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. That is correct, we asked for four hours. We believe we will need all four hours. I should note that the witness upon arrival indicated that he had to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina on Friday -- Friday morning if at all possible. We would request at this time if on Thursday we could switch to morning as opposed to the afternoon if it's possible. I understand Judge Antonetti is sitting in on the Seselj case on Thursday. If we could swap, if that is possible, I'm not demanding, I'm just making this request, this would allow the witness to catch an afternoon flight in order to make it to Sarajevo or Herzegovina where he has some rather important business concerning his current position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Unless I'm mistaken, I believe that we are sitting in the morning, so that should not pose a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe we're sitting in the afternoon, but if we're sitting in the morning that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well. We'll do our utmost to fulfil your request. If there are no other issues to deal with, we will now call the witness into the courtroom. I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. You understand French? Very well. Could you tell me your first and last names and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Martin Raguz, the 2nd of March, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Stolac, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently a representative in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I graduated in political science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a Tribunal with regard to the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time in the Tribunal. I gave a statement in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now. I'll provide you with some information first. First of all, you will have to answer questions that Mr. Karnavas, whom you have surely met, will put to you. Once this stage has been completed, the other members of the Defence representing other accused may also put questions to you as part of their cross-examination. The four Judges who are sitting before you may also intervene and put additional questions to you; this will depend on the documents. Once this has been completed, once this has been done, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will also put questions to you as part of the cross-examination; and if necessary, Mr. Karnavas may put additional questions to you, may re-examine you. We'll do our best to make sure that you can return to your country on Friday because we are aware of the fact that you have other tasks to deal with there. Try and answer the questions very clearly and precisely. If you don't understand the sense of the question, ask the person who is putting the question to you to rephrase it. And every one and a half hours we'll have a break. In an hour and 20 minutes, we'll have a short 20-minute break. If at any point during the proceedings you don't feel well, don't hesitate to ask us for a break. Naturally, the Chamber is to here to deal with any requests that you may have. You've just taken the solemn declaration, which means you are testifying on behalf of justice. This means that in the following days you shouldn't have contact, any more contact, with the Prlic Defence. I wanted to point this out to you. Having said that, I will now give the floor to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Raguz. I'm going to begin by asking you some general questions about your background before we go into the relevant documents that we have set out for your testimony. If you could please just tell us very briefly the education that you have received.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Having completed secondary school in Stolac, which is where I was born, I graduated in political science at the Zagreb University in 1980. I then attended the same university and completed two post-graduate courses there, but my profession now is that of a political scientist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just very briefly I want to cover your professional background. We're mostly interested in your background from 1991 and thereafter, but if you could briefly tell us after graduating the sorts of posts that you held.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Well, first of all when I returned to Stolac I worked in the Stolac local administration, I worked there for three years; and then in 1984 I went to Sarajevo. I stayed there. And in 1991, which is the year you mentioned, I became a professional consultant, I went to work in the Association of the Socialist Youth, the youth organization, that's what it was commonly called in the former Yugoslavia, or rather, in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. I held that position until the end of the 1980s, just before the democratic changes in Yugoslavia. That organization in Bosnia and Herzegovina in fact became the first alternative in that regime in relation to the communist party in power at the time. And in that organization the -- there was the appearance of the liberal democratic party and my first political position was held in that party. I was its deputy president. And as events unfolded, as the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I stayed in Sarajevo, whereas other members of the party leadership left Sarajevo. I remained in Sarajevo. And when the aggression was launched against Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the course of the aggression I participated as a representative of that party in forming a joint government. It was formed by representatives of seven or eight parties, and I was a member of that first government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was representing that party. I was the minister for work, social affairs, and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, if you could help us because the dates may be important. And I'm going to ask you to slow down a little bit because the translators are going to -- are working very hard. So at what point in time were you appointed to this particular ministry?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: In 1992, I think it was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And for how long were you in that position ?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I was in that position officially until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could please describe for the Trial Chamber what exactly this ministry did, in more particular what exactly you did during that period.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Well, my main task within that ministry was in fact to deal with the humanitarian catastrophe and the consequences suffered by Bosnia and Herzegovina in its capital, Sarajevo. Given the fact that at the time when the government was formed in June Sarajevo was under blockade, it had been attacked and it was under a blockade, communications were minimal or non-existent but that ministry at the beginning established a system together with local and international humanitarian organizations a system to deal with the terrible humanitarian situation. We had been surrounded, conditions were terrible, shelling was constant, and under such conditions there were about 100.000 people, women and children, who were constantly under sniper fire. It was necessary to somehow ensure that aid was distributed and to satisfy the minimum needs of the population. We concentrated on Sarajevo given that it was impossible for us to communicate with other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question. To what extent was your ministry, since this is the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to what extent was your ministry able to provide this sort of assistance to other areas that were in need of such assistance during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Given what I have said with regard to the situation in Sarajevo, given the impossibility of establishing communications, and given the fact that we were under a total blockade, the means that we had at our disposal were very limited, almost minimal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that you were in Sarajevo. Did there come a time when you left Sarajevo; and if so, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: The first time I left as a member of the government was in August 1992. I was then a member of the governmental representation or delegation of the first conference on victims of war. It was organized in Geneva by the UNHCR and under the auspices of the High Commissioner, Ms. Sadako Ogata. Afterwards, I returned to Sarajevo and subsequently I left for similar reasons and I would then return in the new year, 1993, I left to see my family whom I hadn't seen, and I went to Bosnian new year then. And then in 1993, given that the government which I was a member had an office of its own in Zagreb in the Republic of Croatia, I thought that given the fact that humanitarian needs were increasing, I thought that I would be able to work there more efficiently. And so I spent that period in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just to be more precise for the record, when was it that you left Sarajevo and relocated to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I can't say that I moved there because on 14 occasions, together with my family, I had changed my address during the war and after the war. But during that period, I think it was the 28th of December, 1992, it was just before the new year in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were in Zagreb still working in that capacity, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly you were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Well, during that period of time in the Republic of Croatia, apart from the displaced persons who had moved within Croatia itself, given the fact that war was waged in Croatia, well there were 100.000 refugees and Bosnia and Herzegovina there. Most of them passed through the Republic of Croatia. They would stay there, they would be provided with first aid, they would be given the means of communicating with their families or with humanitarian and other organizations. So I had contact with this population, with refugees and displaced persons, I had contact with international organizations who provided aid and assistance, and I had certain other duties to carry out. I had signed certain agreements for the government since it wasn't possible for these agreements to be signed in Sarajevo. These agreements concerned obtaining financial means for the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I could ask you, how long did you keep that position, this is working for the government of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: As I have already said, the government workload, given the political situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina was becoming more and more complex -- well, its workload was increasing; and that government had concentrated on one part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and on the main political interests that were established in Sarajevo. So at the beginning of 1993 my engagement in the government had been significantly reduced because of that governmental position. In a certain sense, instead of taking advantage of the opportunity to work more efficiently outside of Sarajevo for the needs of the government and for the needs of the population and of that country, we in a certain sense were pushed aside. And during that period, spring 1993, just before the conflict broke out between the Armija and the HVO, well it was in fact already quite clear that that government was conducting policies that were mostly determined in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just -- if you could keep your answers a little more direct. When were you officially relieved or you left your position with the ministry for the BiH government? If you could give us a month and a year, that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I think it was in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And prior to -- prior to July 1993, if I understand your previous answer, you were essentially pushed aside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to July 1993, did you at any point become engaged with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: On the 31st of May, 1993, I was appointed as the deputy head of the office for refugees and displaced persons of the HZ HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And did there come a time when you actually became the head of the office; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 1st of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we're going to speak more in-depth about this period, but I want to fast-forward a little bit. If you could tell us up until which point in time were you the head of the office. You were appointed on December 1st, 1993, up until what point did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I headed the office until the establishment of the government of the Federation after the Washington Agreement when I was elected deputy minister in the government of the republic and the Federation for refugees and social welfare in Sarajevo again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Again I want to take it step by step to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands your background. So you held this position as head of the office after we have the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna until the establishment of the Federation, and then you begin working for the Federation and more or less doing the same thing, the same sort of work. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how long did you hold that position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I held that position until the peace agreement for Bosnia and Herzegovina was signed, initialled in Dayton and signed in Paris, at the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And after that, did you in any way continue to function or to carry out functions dealing with humanitarian assistance and aid, displaced persons, and what have you for Bosnia and Herzegovina, for the state, that is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, in the year 2000 I was elected the first minister of the then-formed ministry for human rights and refugees at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Council of Ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, let's go back, if we can, to on or about May 31st, 1991, just very briefly if you could tell us what exactly you found when you got to Herceg-Bosna. And please keep in mind -- I mean 1993, I'm sorry. Please keep in mind that what we're going to try to do for the Trial Chamber is to split your time into two periods, one when you're the deputy and then later on when you're the head of the office. This way it might be more convenient for the Trial Chamber to follow your testimony. So upon your arrival when you are appointed as deputy head of the office, could you please tell us what exactly you found.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I found an extremely complicated humanitarian situation which became more and more complicated as time went by, in view of the fact that the war was intensifying and in view of the overall difficult humanitarian situation throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, as most of the people tried to save themselves through the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and through which most of the refugees were received and supported, they received the first instructions as to the possibilities for further accommodation and the situation as regards aid. In general, all this mostly went through the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So the number of refugees increased on a daily basis coming from all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. The humanitarian needs increased, and military operations were escalating throughout the territory. And I came across people who under those difficult circumstances were working to try and deal with the situation, to try and help the people. And in view of the graveness of the war and the ineffectiveness of the government institutions in Sarajevo with respect to the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this forced people to self organize themselves and to link together. And therefore my arrival there also was in the interest of strengthening the system and for the government and the bodies of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to manage to deal with the challenges they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If I could ask you, who was the head of the office at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Mr. Darinko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how large of a staff did you find and what sort of resources, financial resources or other sorts of resources, did Mr. Tadic have at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: There were about 25 to 30 people who were organized to work in five departments for care, for humanitarian aid, for relations with humanitarian organizations, for reconstruction, and the office had very limited resources at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now if I could just -- a couple of quick questions. First of all, we know by this point in time you've had some experience with humanitarian aid. When you first got your position in Sarajevo with the ministry, with this particular ministry, could you please tell us to what -- what sort of specific experience did you have in this field?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in Sarajevo, I cannot say that I had a great deal of experience in the area. But the war in Sarajevo and the clash with the reality of the situation in Sarajevo and the search for solutions under those circumstances gave me the experience to deal with those matters more effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So it was basically learning on the job, as they say; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Herceg-Bosna, did you notice whether the international community, whether the -- whether it was an NGO or whether it was any of the UN organizations, did they provide any technical assistance, that is, perhaps some personnel there to assist in giving guidance?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, there were -- they were there. Most of those humanitarian organizations were represented, especially the key ones like the UNHCR, the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: But they too developed their own infrastructure, and as far as I'm aware they did not provide that infrastructure and put it at the disposal of the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very briefly we're going to go through the documents, but obviously from your experience both as deputy and head of the office if you could please explain to us how the office was organized, first, within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. How did it fit in in the organizational chart sense?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: The office was founded pursuant to a decision of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as an office, which was to ensure the implementation of the decree which was also adopted relative to the status of refugees, displaced -- and displaced persons in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And later, as the whole structure gradually improved its organization in view of the conditions, it became an office of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for refugees and displaced persons. A similar organization, I must say, was established within the framework of the ministry in Sarajevo, where apart from the ministry towards the end of 1992 a directorate was established for refugees as a government agency for humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you could please describe to us the difference between an office and a department, because we know that there were various departments in HVO and you told us that this was an office.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So could you please describe the difference between the two and also tell us to whom you were responded -- the office was responsible to directly.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: The head of the office, first Mr. Tadic, and then later on when I was nominated we were not members of the government with any rights to make decisions. We were not equal to ministers in the government. We attended government meetings, especially when the agenda items referred to the activities of the office. And by decision, we were responsible to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you say "to the government," was there any particular individual or was it this collective body, which of the two? If you could be rather very concrete on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: The government as a body which made decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So, if -- I want to make sure I'm very clear and I don't want to lead you in any way, but was it the government which would issue a decision to the office, and then based on that decision, the collective decision taken, it would be the office that would execute it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, we're going to go through the documents, but as I understand it there is rather concrete legal instruments that set out the rights and obligations of the office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it also, there were rules as far as how this office were to operate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us who drafted those rules -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas, there's one point I would like to clarify. Witness, it appears that the office was not attached to a ministry. Is that the case or -- that is to say was it directly under the authority of the government or was it attached to a ministry -- to a department, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was independent, but it relied on the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare but it was independent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you please explain what "relied" to means? What do we have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This department made certain decisions regulating the work of humanitarian organizations, their registration, record-keeping. And in view of the fact that we directly communicated with humanitarian organizations, it was only logical that we needed to cooperate closely with respect to these issues. But we were not subordinated to that ministry, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would mean that the ministry could not give you any directives or orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On its own, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I think we need to be careful, Mr. Raguz, describing departments as ministries. I think it's departments, so if we could use the same terminology so not to confuse some of us. So this office, as I understand it, is directly responsible to this collective body called government?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Correct, and I accept your suggestions and advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could -- I think we can start now by just going through the documents. It may be a good time since we have lots to go through. The first chapter, if you want to call it that, deals with -- deals with the RBiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, if you could assist us here for a second. And, Your Honours, we have -- we're providing you with a list in the chronological order. It's only one binder. We're providing you with a list so that -- to make it as easy as possible. I think it won't be that confusing. This was just prepared and we hope that the list does provide some assistance, so any feedback would be welcomed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The first document I want to go through is 1D 02734, if you could look at it, sir, and -- that would be the first document in your binder. We can see it's from Oslobodjenje. We all know what it is. It's dated 18 June 1991, and obviously this is from a press conference of the liberal party of which you told us you were the vice-president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to focus the attention of the Trial Chamber at the very last paragraph in this document, this is for the purposes of letting the Trial Chamber know your position, your stated position back then in 18 June, 1991, and let me just read off this and then I'll ask a question. It is reported that: "Martin Raguz, vice-president of the Liberal Party of BH, spoke of the over-casual use of concepts of dissociation, cantonisation, or regionalisation of BH. Citing the constitution of the Socialist Republic of BH and amendments made to it, Raguz said that it was well-known that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a sovereign republic and that its territory was indivisible." Was that your stated position back then, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but I must make a comment if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: There is no doubt at all that then, and even today, I was in favour of respecting the integrity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent democratic state and in favour of respect for its integrity. But then and now I was in favour of a democratic constitution which would regulate internal relations within Bosnia and Herzegovina on the basis of the principle of equality [Realtime transcript read in error "quality"] of nations and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could just get this out of the way because there was a question as late as last month concerning what is a constituent person or what is a constituent nation. If you could tell us what is it when we're talking about nations or constituent peoples in BiH so we have one clear definition?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I absolutely believe that we do have such a definition. In the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and also in annex 4 of the Dayton Peace Agreement in its preamble, it is clearly stated that the peoples, that is, Croats, Bosniaks, Serbs, together with all the other citizens constitute Bosnia and Herzegovina, which means that they are the constituents of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 00942 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps for the -- the record on line 18 you find the principle of "quality of nation," it should probably be "equality" but there might have been a misunderstanding so it's better to put that clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Raguz, on 18 it talks -- it says here -- the record says the principle of quality of nations. That's --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Equality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And of course that principle, since it was mentioned, is rather important because not every nation has the same percentage of population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if a nation, let's just say the Croat nation which I believe had 17.2 or 3 per cent, for it to be equal mechanisms had to be within the constitution that would ensure that within the distribution of political and administrative offices the Croats would receive their proportionate representation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That is correct. According to the official census of 1991 there was 17.8 per cent of the population were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 00942, and we've seen this document before, Mr. Raguz, so we don't have to dwell on it too much. It's dated, if we look at the second page, on 26 June 1992, and we see that it is a platform for activities of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in conditions of war. My first question is: You being the vice-president of the liberal party might know whether your party was in any way involved in the drafting, or overseeing the drafting, or participating in the drafting in any way of this particular platform.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: This platform was adopted by the then-Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had already changed and it had a dominant role. I can't remember that the parties had any real possibility of influencing that platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just very briefly, if we look at the second paragraph on the first paragraph under topic 1: "What kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Let me read one sentence and ask you to provide us with some input. It says here: "The Republic is constituted on the principle of civil parliamentary democracy, which above all implies a market economy, party pluralism, and human rights and freedoms." Now, based on that could you -- well, first could you please analyse that for us and tell us in your opinion what exactly is being said in this particular sentence on what kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina there should be.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I think that the passage you have just read and which relates to the principles of parliamentary civil democracy, this term "civil," in view of the nature of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was superfluous. It would have been quite sufficient to say the principles of parliamentary democracy because in those days in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even today, there is fierce political dispute regarding the constitutional nature of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This term, "civil," in Bosnia and Herzegovina implies the principle one man/one vote, which is a precondition of a unitary form of regulation of the state, and we have already said that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina is a state of three peoples within which the national interests cannot be achieved merely through the concept of one man/one vote. So that this platform, even though it was meant to be the political basis for the activities of the Presidency and the government at the time, in this way reduced the political scope and possibility for the broader commitment of representatives of other parties and, I would also add, of other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 01773, again we've seen this document before, but I just want to dwell on a couple of points if you have it. We see that this is a platform for regulating the relationship with the Republic of Croatia. And if we look on the very first page, under item number 3 it says: "Regulating the positions for the centres for acceptance of humanitarian and other assistance arriving to Bosnia and Herzegovina through the territory of Croatia, its storage, keeping, and transport." Under item 4 it talks about opening an embassy in Zagreb, under item 5: "Regulating the status of refugees from RBiH on the territory of Croatia as well as delivering of humanitarian assistance and [sic] refugees." And under item 6 it talks about "the Republic of Croatia to provide assistance to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in food and construction material." One simple question, based on your experience at the time having lived in Zagreb and then later on working as the deputy and then later the head of the office in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, were you able to observe whether the Republic of Croatia did indeed provide the sort of assistance that this particular platform was requesting from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: When I have a look at this document now, I think that all these items, opening humanitarian logistics centres, embassies, and regulating the status of refugees, assisting Bosnia and Herzegovina, et cetera, I think the Republic of Croatia did all these things and it cooperated with Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to carry out what has been stated under these items. I could draw your attention to the agreement between the president of Croatia and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic. The Bosnian and Herzegovinian side stated that Croatia had gone beyond its own possibilities in contributing to the reception of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Mr. President, is it possible the witness could indicate the date or the time-frame in which this platform and the previous exhibit were being circulated because I've been looking. I'm not seeing a date on this, and I think it would be useful at least to know in general terms the time-frame that these platforms relate to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may very briefly, Your Honour, the first document which is 1D -- pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It's dated 26 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just about to say that. The second platform which I assume Mr. Stringer is mostly concerned about, doesn't have a date; however, however, if we look at the next document which is what Mr. Raguz already began to talk about, which is July 21, 1992, there we would see that some of these issues that are being addressed in the platform for regulating relations with Republic of Croatia are actually -- they come into this particular agreement. I don't know if that assists Mr. Stringer; however, we will also see later on some documents -- we will also see later some documents that show that logistics centres were, indeed, established. Also, I should point out that Mr. Primorac who testified here, Judge Trechsel, you were absent at the time, did indeed comment on this as well. I don't believe Mr. Stringer was in court at the time. But I believe it would be roughly -- you know, if we -- the way we see these documents based on Mr. Primorac is that one deals with the other. So if I could go on to the next document, and then if Mr. Stringer still has an objection or a concern, we can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we can look at the next document, P 00339, and this is the agreement on friendship and cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republic of Croatia dated July 21 1992, we've seen this on many occasions but it never hurts to go over some of it. At the very -- on the second page under item 1 it talks about the establishment of a constitutional political system of the country that would be based on constituent units in the establishments of which due account would be taken on national, historical, cultural, economic traffic and other elements. If we go to item 3 which is on the following page, there, as Mr. Raguz as already indicated, in this agreement it says: "The state delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina," that would be Izetbegovic and others, "expressed their gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for having received and provided for refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina beyond the capacity of the Republic of Croatia." Then the next -- the very next paragraph, still within item 3 it says that: "... the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will cooperate in providing for refugees in the Republic of Croatia and other countries collection of humanitarian and financial aid, construction of refugee centres in safe zones in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the return of refugees from the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And I believe that's all we need to address at this particular time with this particular witness. Sir, when we look at this friendship and cooperation agreement, in particular this item 3 that I've just spoke about or just read, to your understanding was -- was this part of the agreement materialised between BiH and the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Are you referring to item 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm referring to item 3, item 3, item 3 -- item 6 talks about the armed component. I'm not -- we've discussed this, but item 3, what I read out, where Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia will cooperate in providing -- now, based -- because we're dealing with matters that you were directly involved in.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: You're referring to this document 00339, item 3; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Throughout that period of time, regardless of how difficult the situation was, how difficult the subsequent conflicts were, action was taken with regard to all these issues. It's true that the logistics centres in Croatia for gathering humanitarian aid for Bosnia and Herzegovina were established in Ploca, in Split, in Rijeka, in Zagreb, and through these centres it was possible to obtain the greatest percentage, the greatest amount, of humanitarian aid for Bosnia and Herzegovina. All other logistical activities for Bosnia and Herzegovina were carried out through the Republic of Croatia and the return of refugees to Bosnia and Herzegovina was mostly carried out through the Republic of Croatia from the Republic of Croatia. These are facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, which is 1D 01935, 1D 01935, I believe we've seen this document as well. On page 1 we can see from the second paragraph that it says: "... proceeding from the Agreement on Friendship and Cooperation between the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia of 21 July," that is the document that we have just seen, "and following talks between the delegations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia which were held on 21 September 1992 in New York during the 47th Session of the General Assembly of the United Nations ..." If we look at the last line on this page: "... have agreed to sign this annex," and if we turn the page and look at the annex and just to focus our attention on item 2, again reinforcing what you indicated before, it says here: "Once more we underline the need to increase efforts in order to find a political solution to end the war and to further the principle of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an equal and integral community of three constituent peoples." Looking at item 2, is that what -- is this the stated position of the Croats as far as you -- as far as you know, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That's correct. That was the principle -- also referred to the referendum in which the will of the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina was put to a test. The Croats opted for this approach, in fact, for the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand you correctly - and of course this is already -- these are already facts in evidence in your testimony, that is, under item -- if we look at number 2 it certainly does not comport with the platform that we looked at, which was 1D 00942, that one section that we read, the second document. In other words where it talks about a civil parliamentary democracy is certainly not consistent with item 2 of the annex to the agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Well, the platform doesn't contain such explicit provisions on the character of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is why I said that it was limited in relation to its possible effects. This was the foundation at the time, and it's also the foundation for future stable relationships in Bosnia and Herzegovina and for a future stable Bosnia and Herzegovina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one item that, again since we're on the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that I wanted to cover and discuss with you very briefly, perhaps you could give us a comment on, and it comes from Lord Owen's book, and it's on 1D 01552, it's a rather discrete issue, it's on -- if we look at the third page of this particular document and in English if you see, Your Honours, at the left side of the third page, 264, I'm referring to that particular passage up there, the first -- here Lord Owen is commenting and he's saying that: "When I asked Izetbegovic, that is, why he did not let Muslim children and their mothers leave Sarajevo, he retorted that the British would never have let them leave London during the Blitz and seemed genuinely surprised when I told him how Churchill's government arranged for children not only to leave London but to go as far afield as Canada." If you could tell us, based on your experience having lived in Sarajevo, albeit until the end of 1992, whether -- what if -- what was the policy of the government or Izetbegovic's policy, if you were aware of, and whether we can rely on what Lord Owen is telling us here as far as what Izetbegovic's strategy was.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: As I've already said when describing the humanitarian situation in Sarajevo at the beginning of the war -- well, this situation was extremely difficult. All I can do is repeat this. We all know that Sarajevo was encircle for several years. The longest air corridor was established for providing humanitarian aid after the Berlin air corridor a lot of innocent people were killed, a lot of women and children were killed. Whether this was politically necessary, well I wouldn't want to go into that issue. But it is a fact that the government in Sarajevo wanted the local and international public to focus on such matters for their own political objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 00898, again we've seen this document but perhaps you could help us out a little bit. This is a decision. It's dated 17 November 1992 by the then-president of the government of the RBiH, Mile Akmadzic. And in the decision it appoints and authorises Dr. Jadranko Prlic, the president of the Croatian Defence Council, to represent the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a number of ways. And if we look at under item 2 at these little bullet points it talks about: "Achieve full cooperation with logistic centres in the territory of Republic of Croatia and the RBiH government ..." The next bullet point: "Maintain all contacts with relevant organs of the Republic of Croatia in connection with the flow of goods and people." Next: "Cooperate -- coordinate all measures issues by the RBiH Government and the Croatian Defence Council ..." and so on. Based on your -- prior to arriving to Herceg-Bosna, did you have any contact with Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions I was a member of the government that appointed and authorised Dr. Jadranko Prlic to deal with issues that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, before coming -- before coming -- I want to make sure that I'm clear with your answer. While you were serve -- while you were with the ministry for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you told us that in May 31, I believe, 1993 you left Zagreb. And so you were in Zagreb approximately from January until the end of May. During that period did you have any contact with Dr. Jadranko Prlic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, during that period of time and while I was in Sarajevo, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us ever so briefly the -- how did you find Jadranko Prlic? How did he behave in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I would say that the government appointed Dr. Jadranko Prlic for a number of reasons, first and foremost because it was possible for him to work outside of Sarajevo, to work more effectively; and secondly, because it was obvious that he was quite capable to organize matters, also when he was deputy head of the executive committee in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we now -- and I'm told that the translation was a bit off, and let me pose the same question. Perhaps you can give us the answer again because I don't want to lead you in any way as far as what you might have said. The question was basically: How did you find Dr. Jadranko Prlic? How did he behave in the capacity that he was serving, that is, as president of the HVO he was now given a mandate by the government of the RBiH to assist in certain issues which of course touched upon issues that you were working with at the time.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said. I think that the government had good reasons to appoint Dr. Prlic since he was good at organizing matters, and this appointment was carried out - I can see this now - in the autumn of 1992. This is on the basis of what the Croatian Defence Council had done to receive refugees, organize humanitarian aid, so the organization was to have a broader function for the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina, given the fact that Dr. Prlic even before the war and at the beginning of the war demonstrated that he had all the necessary qualities to carry out such duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, if we could go on to the next chapter unless the Trial Chamber wishes to have a break at this point. I leave it to -- we're not going to finish within the next ten minutes but I can continue if I can get some guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a break now. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume with the hearing. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document that I want to show you, Mr. Raguz, is actually in the previous chapter, I omitted to mention it, it's 1D 01943, 1D 01943 very briefly, and I'll connect this later on. This is a letter from President Tudjman to the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, dated 12 February 1993. And if we look at the second paragraph it says: "In order for this cooperation to be achieved, I propose that the Ministries of Foreign Affairs immediately take necessary steps to establish bilateral and multilateral committees for every branch of the economy." And it goes on. To your understanding, did the two ministers of foreign affairs, that is, for Bosnia-Herzegovina and for the -- for Croatia, did they get involved in issues related to what you were eventually involved in in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I think that they played significant role and that they got involved in these issues too and the issues that are referred to in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the two foreign ministers that I'm speaking of, that would have been Mr. Silajdzic for Bosnia-Herzegovina and Dr. Granic for the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if we go to the next document, 1D 01232 and the next series of documents we'll be dealing with -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question to this document. Witness, have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Let me go back to the document. Can we return to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is document 1943.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correspondence between presidents or the presidents of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina was officially public, so this was accessible to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This does not exactly answer my question. My question was whether you personally have ever seen this letter before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is correspondence between presidents. I wasn't a member of the Presidency, so I didn't receive such correspondence. But I believe that it is authentic. I'm familiar with this correspondence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps you can or you cannot answer the question. What puzzles me is that in a letter from the president of Croatia to the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the suggestion is made to establish bilateral, and now comes the enigmatic formulation, or multilateral committees. Do you have any ideas, any suggestions, what the multilateral side might refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do have an idea. I have a clear idea of the fact. Both countries had been affected by the war. Both countries had a need to carry out reconstruction, to cooperate in all fields, so that concerns their economy, infrastructure, energy, and everything else. So this is all placed in the broader context, the Alps, the Adriatic, the Carpathians, the Danube, we can see that this is the official policy of all countries in the region and of the European Union regard to that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Thank you, that's quite convincing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go to the next document. As I've indicated, we'll be dealing with a series of documents on the laws on displaced persons and refugees. It's 1D 1232, 1D 01232, if you have it, sir, and we can see from the preamble that this relates to the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And if we look at the very last page, for the record it's dated 6 October 1992 and we see the name of Ejup Ganic, who was deputised for the president of the Presidency, and you could confirm that Mr. Ganic at this point was a member of the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just were you familiar with this particular piece of legislation at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, it was issued by the government I was a member of, and this was officially declared by the Presidency, the War Presidency, it was a decree law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we don't have to go through the entire document because we'll be able to do that on our own, but I thought perhaps we would touch upon a couple of issues that might be of some importance. If we could look at, for instance, Article 17, and in particular what I'm interested in where at the very last part of the sentence it talks about persons over 18 years of age. If you could just look at Article 17 and please tell us what exactly does Article 17 stand for?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Article 17 relates to the obligation of the competent body that issued decisions on the status of displaced individuals, and it had to inform the responsible or the competent organ of individuals of 18 years of age. So the municipal organ had to be informed of obligations that individuals over 18 years of age had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to Article 23 it says here: "The competent state organ that has summoned a displaced person for military or work obligation shall inform of the summons the district office of the municipality in the areas which the displaced persons has his or her place of residence." And before looking or commenting on Article 23 we should also look at the previous article, Article 22 which says: "The rights under this decree of a person who has been recognised the status of a displaced persons shall cease when such a person is summoned by the competent state organ for military or work obligation if for the duration of such obligation he/she receives remuneration according to special regulations." So if you could comment on these two articles because it would seem that perhaps those who are of military age are seen to have a different status?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That's correct. Individuals who have work or military obligation and as a result have other rights -- well, their rights are curtailed pursuant to this decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, was it possible under this decree for someone to be both a displaced person if, for instance, he was within the age -- the military age and had a particular obligation -- a military obligation? In other words, could he be 18, 19, 20 years old and say he wished to enjoy the status of being a displaced person but simply refused or didn't want to participate in his military obligation, you know, sit out the war as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you if we look at Article 27 -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you allow me just an additional question. Reference is made to summons here. Can you tell the Chamber whether this means an individual summons addressed to the person in question by name or does it include general summonses, all male persons between that and that age are called under arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a general approach that was taken, so you can see here that the municipalities or district offices that are referred to in this decree passed by the government of the republic in charge of regulating status issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And can you please tell us whether there was a general mobilisation announced in BiH; and if so, at what point?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: It was announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you give us a date?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Now, exactly when --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about a year, can you give us a year? Was it 1991? 1992? 1993? 1994?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't in 1991 because we were late in many things. So I believe that this was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at just very briefly at Article 27, the third paragraph, it says here that: "Displaced persons may be accommodated in reception facilities, social centres, or host families." If you could tell us, what is a reception facility?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Excuse me, but could you repeat which article we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The article was 27 and it's the third paragraph, it's only one line.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: The reception facilities were places where the persons were initially received, that is, the persons who were expelled or displaced. From these reception centres to collectives, to host families. This is the whole spectrum of possibilities for accommodation of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go back now to Article 21 where it talks about refugee status of a person from a war-ridden area would cease, and if we look at under item 3: "If he/she refuses the offered organized accommodation or other forms of organized assistance ..." If you could please explain that to us. I mean, why couldn't somebody simply demand to be in an apartment, a sea-side hotel, or some other convenient location as opposed to being placed in a centre with other people, perhaps less convenient, less accommodating?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: This means that the bodies in charge of the reception and the regulation of the status of displaced persons and refugees, and these were mainly at the level of municipalities, they would have enormous requests and problems with respect to accommodation and they had to investigate enormous efforts to find appropriate accommodations. So it is quite understandable for this paragraph 3 to figure here, which says that -- which refers to organized necessary accommodation or temporary accommodation, because that was the only accommodation that it was possible to offer people at the time. That is what the conditions were like in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01410, 1D 01410, we see this is a decision on matters concerning the status of citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. It's dated 24 September 1992, and we see that at the time the prime minister was Jure Pelivan. Just a couple of points. If we look at Article -- well, Roman numeral I, it says: "The Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia," it says: "Shall approve departure to other countries to citizens of RBH with the status of displaced persons or refugees and compulsory military or work service in the territory of Croatia ..." and it goes on. Could you please tell us why was the embassy, to your knowledge, involved? Why was it -- should it have been involved in this matter or these matters?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: There were agreements between the two countries that we have already referred to, agreements on cooperation in the area of humanitarian affairs between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in dealing with the status of refugees, and one of the decisions is the one here, whereby the return was sought of the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were under military obligation and the intention of the decision was to have them returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is under Roman numeral IV. Because a large number of people benefitting from the status of refugees wanted to leave on their own initiative, disregarding their military obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And under -- if we look at Roman numeral IV, and that was my next question and I'm gratified that you went to it, it talks about collection centres for the organized return of citizens to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina with military work obligations. And if we look at the locations now, it talks about: "... Zenica, Tuzla, Visoko, Jablanica, Konjic, and other locations named by the Ministry of Defence." If you could please tell us to your understanding, these particular locations, who was controlling them at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: These locations, Zenica, Tuzla, Visoko, Jablanica, and Konjic were under the control of the Armija, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, were men of military age actually sent back from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to fulfill their military obligations based on this particular piece of legislation? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were. To what extent and in what numbers, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we look at the next document P 00 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this document, which to me is of great interest, first of all at the time, you yourself, did you have any personal knowledge of this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this period of time, I was still a minister in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I didn't have direct knowledge of this decision but I have looked at it and it contains the same provisions as those passed by the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When one reads the four chapters of this decision, a jurist could come to the following conclusion. First of all, it appears that there are citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia and who, if they don't return to Bosnia and Herzegovina, should have the status of refugees in the Republic of Croatia. This is what paragraph 2 says. Was that in line with the will of the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina to have a legal status of refugees in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chapter 2 only says that the return of refugees and displaced persons should be made possible, those who are residing in the territory of Herceg-Bosna to the municipalities in which the security situation allows it. So it doesn't refer to anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness is looking at the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going document by document and the President is referring to 1D --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- 1D 01410. So unless I indicate that we're moving to another document, we'll stick with -- so if you could kindly look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, I thought we'd finished with this document and we were moving on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was still talking about the first document, 1D 01410.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. Karnavas for realizing this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me which paragraph of this decision you were referring to because I was looking at another document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Chapter 2. I was referring to chapter 2, which says that: "The citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who cannot return to Bosnia and Herzegovina, either because it is impossible to travel or for reasons of safety, shall be awarded refugee status in the territory of the Republic of Croatia." And therefore my question is whether the government in Sarajevo, wasn't it encouraging Zagreb to grant them refugee status and thereby leave in Croatia certain citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as chapter 2 appears to indicate, which would explain the role of the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia. Is that the way one could read this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one could. So chapter 2 does provide for the possibility for the embassy in Zagreb, pursuant to this provision, to further regulate the status and rights of refugees depending on the transport or security situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, I go back to paragraph 1, a text may mean a lot of things but it appears that the refugees who are in the Republic of Croatia may leave for other countries, but it would appear that the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that case needs to approve such travel. Does that mean that this document envisages a mechanism for the departure of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina who are temporarily in Croatia and who might leave for other countries, Denmark or Switzerland, France, or I don't know where, but on condition that the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina approves such a departure? Is that what this text indicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I add a little question, referring to paragraph, numeral II Roman. We read the words: "... return to the free territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." What does that refer to? Which is the free -- which is the not free at that point in time? We are in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the area that I spoke about in the introduction. This is the view from Sarajevo as to what is free territory. I cannot fully interpret what was meant by the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina from that standpoint at that time, but judging by paragraph 4 of this decision you can see which towns are being designated to receive those persons and this speaks for itself, those are Zenica, Tuzla, Visoko, Jablanica, and Konjic, as towns where those people would be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I still have a question in order to finish with this decision, again concerning paragraph 2, and it says that: "Citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are unable to return to the free territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina either because it is impossible to travel or for reasons of safety shall be awarded refugee status," and again I repeat this, "shall be awarded refugee status in the territory of the Republic of Croatia." Now, my question is the following. It seems to me rather strange that a third country, in this case Bosnia and Herzegovina, actually in a -- in this kind of decision makes a reference in imperative that "shall be awarded refugee status" in another country, in a third country, in this case in Croatia, the refugee status. Was it based on a certain agreement between the two governments, but in this case a reference should have been, as a matter of fact, referred to and -- or was it another type of agreement which was not made public? So my question to you, sir, if -- how come that the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina made a decision which was supposed to be actually applied in a territory of another state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your question is quite appropriate. All I can say is that through the logistics centres and this office for refugees which the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina set up in Croatia, they had the ambition to regulate these matters independently, that is, by the organs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without the participation of the Republic of Croatia. Of course there were agreements of a working nature, some of them of a contractual nature, but they should have indicated which ones they're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still a further clarification. You can see that we are interested in these matters. Paragraph 2 refers on -- refers to: "Citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." That is the citizenship irrelevant -- is it correct to read it as being irrelevant with regard to nationality, so that Croats, Serbs, or Bosniaks are equally covered, at least in theory, by this decision; or is there an implied limitation to Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Bosnia and Herzegovina for you, they are citizens in the sense of their citizenship. And if you look at the text, one cannot say that it refers only to Bosniaks but all of them are being advised we see where -- to go we see where in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Raguz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to follow-up on the question of my colleague, it is true that for a jurist to see paragraph 1 where there is an automatic granting of refugee status, one must believe that there were either bilateral agreements or verbal agreements between the ministers of foreign affairs or even between Tudjman and Izetbegovic to regulate the status of these refugees who are in Croatia. Or Mr. Tudjman must have said, We'll give them this status, which would explain why the text leads to the conclusion that this was automatic. Is this acceptable as an interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already answered that question. It is not logical that the status of refugees in the Republic of Croatia should be decided by the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina; it is the state which is hosting the refugees that should decide. Similarly, I also said that Croatia did offer its infrastructure to organize and assist and take care of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is not stated here but it could be implied. Those were days when Croatia had more than a million refugees and displaced persons, of which several hundred thousand from Bosnia and Herzegovina, so that practical moves had their reasons if the aim was to deal with those matters more effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that most of these questions emanate from problems in the translation of this document. Paragraph 2 is definitely incorrectly translated, and it's a serious mistake. According to the original text it follows that paragraph 2 regulates the status for those citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are in Croatia and who already have the status of refugees. And then it is stipulated that if those persons are unable to return to the free territory for transport or safety reasons, so the meaning is quite different, whereas in English it says that those persons shall be awarded -- should be given the status of refugees. So that is quite wrong. It is obvious that the intention of the government is to deal with those who already have the status of refugees in the Republic of Croatia and who are at the time military -- of military age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovacic, you have raised a problem there. Perhaps we can deal with the problem asking the witness to read chapter 2 and then the interpreters can interpret for us. So, Witness, could you read for us chapter 2 in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are situated in the territory of the Republic of Croatia and enjoy the status of refugees are persons who are unable to return to the free territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina due to transport difficulties or for safety reasons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that in the translation that we have just heard it would appear that the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have the status of refugees -- who have this status are the persons who cannot return. That is what is said in the version in your own language, whereas the English translation could be misleading. There's a difficulty which we have tried to overcome. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, thank you, Your Honours, and thank you to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to go back to the question that Judge Trechsel asked and I'm terribly grateful to that question, because if I understand correctly what you indicated based on the question that was asked of you because you pointed to Roman numeral IV, it would appear, since we're talking about citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that would be Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, if they are of military age they are to be sent to collection centres that are provided by the Ministry of Defence to those territories that are for all intents and purposes controlled by only one of the nations, and that is the Muslims at the time, the Army of BiH, Zenica, Tuzla, Visoko, Jablanica, Konjic. Is that correct? Is that my understanding of your answer based on the question posed to you by Judge Trechsel?
